items.note: Sonari village lies about five km from Baretha station on the Sonari Kevtan river, which spews out broken and whole idols when its water dries; idols are kept in village houses.
Most idols are Vishnu avatars; some are in the Vidisha District Archaeology Museum, including a whole Varaha masterpiece and a rescued Vishnu named Vishwa Mohan.
Author says Vishnu idols from Muradpur to Sonari link the region to the Vishnu-worshipping Guptas, five hundred years before Udayadity.
Place about 15 km from Udaipur toward Patari; ruins of Patari show it must have been a developed town in Mauryan and Gupta times (author's reading).
Small old fort called 'Garhi' on a forested hill in Ganj Basoda tehsil, Vidisha district.
Local lore, first thread: the Garhi was a dacoits' base from which demands went out.
Local lore, second thread: a now-desolate village Daulatpur stood below, with markets; how villages became desolate is unexplained.
Local lore, fourth thread: 'Bagdi', a branch of local Rajputs who rebelled against Muslim rulers, lived here in an organised way.
Author speculates 'Gyasi' may be a corrupted 'Gyasuddin', a ruler who sent decrees to collect tax; villagers would see him as a looter (conjecture).
Suggestion to government: compulsory heritage walks for students and tourist circuits covering two or three monuments a day.
Proposals: publications on local history and archaeology in schools, short films, and heritage-themed competitions.
Vivek writes that Udaydit fashioned Udaipur, as a descendant of Bhoj and governor of the kingdom's last edge, and had the Udaysagar built.
Calls the Nilkantheshvar temple a matchless architectural specimen with replicas of the temple arranged one above another from base to spire.
Idols with broken hands and missing heads; marks of blows are clear.
Mosque made from temple remnants; idols stuck behind its stones; half-finished mosque walls in the temple precinct are cited as evidence.
A madrasa took possession of the palace, cultivation began on the Udaysagar, and the temple was gripped by encroachment.
Palace occupied by a madrasa, cultivation on the Udaysagar, encroachment on the temple.
A band of enthusiastic youths organised to make people alert to the heritage and takes visitors to Udaipur every month.
Plan under consideration for grassroots work cherishing heritage and awakening history consciousness, in Dr Mishra's memory.

Malwa in centuries before Christ was known as Dasharna and Avanti; Vidisha centre of eastern Malwa; Udaipur about 70 km from Vidisha, in its prime perhaps the temple-city of the ancient Dasharna kingdom.
Udayeshvar Mahadev called the finest Paramara-era construction in the Bhumija style; scholars say the style arose in Malwa in the Paramara period and spread to other regions.

claim.value: originated in Malwa in the Paramara period (9th-10th century, per this author); spread to Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha, etc.

items.note: A 'private property' notice was found pasted on the ruined remains of the old royal palace.
Local people removed encroachments and cleared the path to the temple; a nearly three-foot-wide cemented road was built through public cooperation.
Author likens the new road to the road to the Deccan, linking the Uttarapath and Dakshinapath, a highway of devotion on which dynasties built temple cities.
Proposal: a Paramara-era temple tourism circuit, bringing in Khajuraho's foreign visitors; Udaipur chapter to begin, Bhojpur already established.
Dr Mishra said the whole of Udaipur could be developed like a heritage town.
Important archaeological wealth lies within five km of Udaipur; houses within 500 m of the temple are built of ancient antiquarian material.

Udayagiri caves, Udaipur and Udaysamudra (about 500 m in front of the temple) are named after Udyadity, mentioned as Bhoj's grandson (pautra) and elsewhere as Bhoj's kinsman; the fifth-century Udayagiri caves were not built by him.
Time to begin the Udaipur chapter of the Paramara-era tourism circuit on a PPP model, with local cooperation.
